strengths: Presents a genuinely novel information-theoretic treatment of weight-only PTQ: under an iid-Gaussian weight model, the paper derives the exact rate-distortion limit via reverse waterfilling, rigorously shows that the standard entropy-coded GPTQ can have an arbitrarily large gap to this limit, and proves the proposed WaterSIC scheme is within a universal 0.255-bit gap of the IT limit for any input covariance (Theorem 3.3, with careful supporting lemmas on lattice flatness and Renyi differential-entropy convergence).

The key algorithmic idea—allocating different quantization rates (grid spacings) to different input-feature columns, mirroring classical waterfilling, combined with entropy coding rather than fixed-range scaling—is simple, well-motivated by the theory, and, to the reviewers' knowledge, not used by prior PTQ methods that apply one rate per layer or per group.

The step from the idealized 'PlainWaterSIC' to the practical 'WaterSIC' algorithm is carefully engineered with multiple well-justified refinements (LMMSE/shrinkage correction, Qronos-style activation-drift correction, residual-stream correction for down-projection layers, alternating row/column rescaler optimization, attention-weighted calibration, adaptive mixing, dead-feature erasure), each with a clear rationale grounded in the underlying loss decomposition.

Extensive empirical validation across four model families/sizes (Llama-3.2-1B, Llama-2-7B, Llama-3-8B, Qwen3-8B) and rates from 1 to 4 bits, compared against many strong and diverse baselines (GPTQ, Huffman-GPTQ/HPTQ, AWQ, QTIP, NestQuant, GPTVQ, QuIP#), consistently showing improved perplexity, largely without any fine-tuning or sophisticated base quantizer/codebook, which strengthens the claim that gains stem specifically from the waterfilling-rate idea.

Thorough ablations (Figs. 7-11) isolate the contribution of each individual technique (residual correction, drift correction, attention weighting, adaptive mixing) via layerwise relative-MSE diagnostics, and additional analyses (compression rate distributions, Zstd/LZMA validation of entropy estimates, KL-divergence comparisons, zero-shot accuracy benchmarks) substantially bolster the credibility and reproducibility of the empirical claims.

The limitations section is honest and specific (no end-to-end fine-tuning integration, no hardware/throughput benchmarking of variable-length decoding, limited model scale), rather than vague or self-serving.
weaknesses: The clean 0.255-bit theoretical guarantee applies only to the idealized 'PlainWaterSIC' under an iid-Gaussian weight assumption and asymptotic (a→∞, high-rate) regime; the actual algorithm deployed in experiments ('full WaterSIC') adds many additional heuristics (drift correction, residual correction, attention weighting, adaptive mixing, dead-feature erasure, diagonal rescalers) that are not covered by the theoretical analysis, so the abstract's framing ('shown to be within a rate gap of 0.255 bits... uniformly over all possible covariance matrices') somewhat overstates what is proven for the method actually evaluated.

The practical pipeline has many moving parts and per-model/per-layer tuned hyperparameters (golden-section search per layer for two mixing coefficients, dead-feature threshold, damping schedules, and model-specific manual interventions such as zeroing specific outlier rows in Qwen3-8B), which raises concerns about robustness/generalization to new architectures without significant additional tuning, and about ease of reproducibility relative to simpler baselines like plain GPTQ or RTN.

Comparisons mix entropy-based and log-cardinality-based rate reporting across methods in the same plots (acknowledged by the authors), which, while transparent, complicates strictly fair comparison to codebook/lattice-based baselines (QTIP, NestQuant, QuIP#, GPTVQ, AWQ) that were not designed for variable-length entropy coding.

No benchmarking of actual inference/decoding throughput or memory overhead of the variable-length entropy-coded representation on real hardware, despite this being central to whether the reported bit-rate gains translate into practical deployment benefits; this is noted as a limitation but leaves the practical significance claims (e.g., 'new SOTA') only partially substantiated for real systems.

No fine-tuning-based baselines (e.g., PV-Tuning, AQLM, YAQA) are directly compared at matched settings, and comparisons for Llama-3-8B at the more standard 4096 context length are deferred to future work, limiting completeness of the SOTA claims relative to the strongest existing extreme-compression methods.

Single-run results without variance/error bars across evaluation metrics, making it harder to assess statistical robustness of the reported improvements, especially at very low bitrates where perplexity is highly sensitive to small changes.

strengths: Novel and rigorous information-theoretic framing of linear-layer PTQ: the paper defines proper (R,D) fundamental limits for weight-only quantization under a Gaussian weight model, derives a waterfilling lower bound, and proves (Theorem 3.3, with full proofs in Appendix A/B) that standard GPTQ can have an unbounded rate gap to this limit while the proposed WaterSIC scheme is within a universal 0.255-bit gap for any input covariance matrix.

The key algorithmic idea -- allocating a different quantization step size per column proportional to 1/ℓ_ii (the Cholesky/innovation scale) rather than a single global step -- is simple, well-motivated by the AMGM argument connecting GPTQ and WaterSIC distortion formulas, and cleanly explains the empirical gains.

Extensive and carefully constructed empirical evaluation: results across five model families (Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen3-8B, Llama-3-8B, Llama-2-7B, Llama-3-70B) and bit rates from 1-4 bits, comparisons against a wide range of strong recent baselines (Huffman-GPTQ/HPTQ, QTIP, NestQuant, AWQ, GPTVQ, QuIP#, AQLM, PV-Tuning, YAQA), plus zero-shot downstream benchmarks and KL-divergence evaluation, consistently showing state-of-the-art or highly competitive results.

Thorough ablations and diagnostics (Appendix E-G): per-technique MSE breakdowns for residual-stream correction, drift correction, attention weighting, and adaptive mixing; empirical verification of the Gaussian-weight assumption via KS tests; verification that entropy estimates translate into real Zstd/LZMA compressed sizes; and sensitivity studies on calibration/finetuning corpus and context length.

Good reproducibility support: full algorithmic pseudocode (Algorithms 1-4), detailed hyperparameter settings, and code release; honest discussion of limitations (loss objective choice, lack of end-to-end throughput benchmarking, scale of models tested).
weaknesses: The clean theoretical guarantee (0.255-bit gap) applies only to the idealized PlainWaterSIC under iid Gaussian weight rows and asymptotic high-rate/large-a limits; the practical algorithm used in experiments (Algorithm 3) layers on many additional heuristics (LMMSE shrinkage, activation-drift correction, residual-stream correction, attention-weighted calibration with per-layer golden-section-optimized mixing coefficients, dead-feature erasure, post-hoc finetuning) that are not covered by the theory, so the strong empirical results cannot be cleanly attributed to the IT-optimality argument alone.

The Gaussianity assumption underlying the whole analysis is checked only via KS-distance goodness-of-fit on a few models (Llama-2-7B, Llama-3-8B, Llama-3.2-1B) and shows non-trivial deviations for wq/wk; the paper does not analyze or bound how such deviations affect the proven 0.255-bit gap in practice.

The practical algorithm has a substantial number of hyperparameters (damping δ, dead-feature threshold τ, mixing parameters ϵ_qr/ϵ_aw optimized per layer via golden search, secant-based rate matching, LMMSE shrinkage) whose joint tuning burden and sensitivity to new architectures is not deeply analyzed, raising some concern about ease of generalization/reproducibility beyond the tested models.

Rate accounting differences between entropy-coded methods (WaterSIC, Huffman-GPTQ) and log-cardinality-based baselines (AWQ, QTIP, NestQuant, QuIP#, GPTVQ) are acknowledged but could still make some cross-method comparisons not fully apples-to-apples, since entropy coding inherently captures distributional savings that fixed-rate codebooks cannot.

No end-to-end latency/throughput results are reported for the variable-length entropy-coded representation, despite this being central to practical deployment; the paper defers this to future work, which somewhat limits the practical significance claims relative to hardware-friendly fixed-rate quantizers.
